To define $ \Delta S_{conf} $ we begin by comparing the adsorption of alkanes in five different zeolite structures: MFI, CHA, TON, FAU, and MOR. Depicted in Figure 2A is the relationship between the entropy of an adsorbed molecule (alkanes and permanent gases) and its gas-phase entropy, where the molecular entropy on the surface never exceeds that in the gas phase. While a significant loss in entropy occurs in all five zeolites, the absolute loss in entropy is distinct for each framework. Adsorbates in TON exhibit the largest loss in entropy upon adsorption, while FAU results in the smallest entropic losses. ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). Predictive capability of confined molecular entropy permits an understanding of the relation with adsorption enthalpy, the ability to computationally screen microporous materials, and an understanding of the role of confinement on the kinetics of molecules in confined spaces.

On the basis of this shape-selective feature , highly effective molecular separations and selective catalytic conversions can be achieved within zeolitic structures that are difficult to accomplish with other materials and/or techniques . $ ^ { 1-3 } $ So far, several shape-selectivity mechanisms have been elucidated and applications identified. $ ^{2-18} $ In common molecular sieving, bulky molecules adsorb preferentially over bulkier species as a result of steric constraints imposed by the zeolites' framework, e.g., linear alkane molecules compared to branched isomers. $ ^{19-23} $ Besides this common adsorption competition based on molecular bulkiness, the reverse phenomenon can also occur, i.e., competitive adsorption in favor of the bulkier species. Experiments revealed preferential adsorption of branched alkanes over their linear isomers on specific zeolites with tubular pore systems such as SAPO-5 and Mordenite. $ ^{24-28} $ Molecular simulations indicated that in such zeolites, depending on conditions, branched alkanes are preferentially adsorbed at the expense of linear isomers. $ ^{29-34} $ The present manuscript discusses the mechanisms of shape selectivity in n- and isoalkane adsorption on zeolite MCM-22. This zeolite with IZA code MWW is a relatively new synthetic material that has an unusual and quite complex pore structure. $ ^{35} $ Its framework is composed of two independent pore systems. The enthalpy and the entropy contributions to the Gibbs free energies were calculated at T = 298 K and partial pressure of 1 atm (101325 Pa). The enthalpy (H) of gas-phase pyridine and acetonitrile molecules is defined as the sum of total electronic energy ( $ E_{el} $), internal vibrational energy ( $ E_{v} $), zero-point vibrational energy (ZPVE), as well as the rotational and translational contributions to the internal energy: $ H = E_{el} + E_{v} + ZPVE + E_{R} + E_{t} $. The corresponding calculated entropies (S) includes translational, ( $ S_{t} $) vibrational, ( $ S_{v} $) and rotational ( $ S_{r} $) degrees of freedom: $ S = S_{t} + S_{v} + S_{r} $. All the considered systems are in singlet state, thus the electronic contribution to the entropy is zero. Since both adsorbed molecules are constrained in the zeolite cavity their entropy contributions in the adsorption complexes were corrected as follows: the translational and rotational degrees of freedom were reduced by 1 and 1.28 [37]. The Gibbs free energies of the zeolite support consist of only vibrational and electronic contributions. The expressions of all enthalpy and entropy contributions can be found in Ref. [38].

The first attempts to describe guest-induced flexibility in zeolites were done using molecular dynamics simulations. $ ^{79-82} $ Rigid zeolitic force fields were dynamically modified using transition state theory to include lattice flexibility, and the results obtained by these models were in good agreement with experimental data. $ ^{79-81,83,84} $ It was shown that framework flexibility in silicalite-1 (MFI-type framework) is responsible for the adsorption of large molecules such as isobutane and heptane with inflection behavior at high loadings, $ ^{80} $ while enhanced self-diffusivity at low loadings of short alkanes (i.e. methane and n-butane) was observed. $ ^{81} $ Framework flexibility is also crucial for aromatics adsorption on MFI zeolite, especially at high pressures. $ ^{84,85} $ While the use of rigid zeolitic models led to the underestimation of the aromatics adsorption in MFI zeolite by a factor of two, $ ^{84,85} $ the use of flexible models to simulate diffusion coefficients of various alkanes in silicalite-1 zeolite resulted in a convergence of experimental and theoretical values. $ ^{86} $ Recently by using in situ integrated differential phase contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy (iDPC-STEM) while adsorbing benzene molecules on MFI zeolite, Xiong et al. showed that the MFI structure goes through severe deformations giving another proof of guest-induced flexibility in zeolites (see Fig. 4). $ ^{87} $

2.4.4. Trapdoor. Traditional diﬀusion models primarily consider two types of interactions: those between guest molecules (guest–guest) and those between guest molecules and the zeolite framework (guest–host). However, when cations are present in the zeolite structure, a third interaction—involving guest molecules, the framework, and cations (guest–host-cation)—must also be accounted for. A striking example of such ternary interactions is the well-known ‘‘molecular trapdoor’’. This phenomenon, also referred to as the ‘‘gating effect’’, describes a unique molecular sieving mechanism in certain zeolites and related porous materi- als. Here, extra-framework cations function as dynamic gate- keepers at pore apertures, selectively controlling molecular diffusion to achieve highly discriminative adsorption and separation.9,147,187 To date, ‘‘trapdoor’’ has been observed in several zeolites, including RHO (DNL-6),188–190 CHA (SAPO-34, SSZ-13),147,191,192 MWF (ZSM-25),149,193 HEU (Clinoptilolite),194

The turnover rates of olefin formation during cyclohexanol (CyOH) dehydration within the autoclave reactor initially increase with the local ionic strength within a micropore, and further decrease along ionic strength promotion, shown as a volcano-shaped dependence of TOFs on the ionic strength of zeolites. In the following appendix , we derive the entropy of adsorption in the case of infinite dilution and show how it may be related to familiar thermodynamic quantities ( cf . eq 5 ) . To begin , we define our adsorption entropy in the limit of infinite dilution via

$$ \Delta s_{\mathrm{ads}}^{\infty}=\lim_{N/V\rightarrow0}\left[\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{ads}}-\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{gas}}\right] $$

$$ =S_{ads}(N=1,V,T)-S_{gas}(N=1,V,T) $$

where the subscripts “ads” and “gas” labels identify the adsorbed (confined) and gas (bulk) phases, respectively. Given the constraints of a fixed number of molecules (N), volume (V), and temperature (T), it is natural to continue working in the canonical ensemble. (As in the main text, lowercase symbols identify intensive molecular or molar properties, whereas the uppercase indicates an extensive property.) For the molecules that we examine in this work (e.g., rigid molecules with no internal degrees of freedom), the canonical partition function Q may be expressed as

$$ \begin{aligned}Q(N,V,T)&=Q_{trans}(N,V,T)Q_{rot}(N,V,T)\\&\quad\times Z(N,V,T)\end{aligned} $$

where $ Q_{trans} $ and $ Q_{rot} $ are the translational and rotational partition functions (which are unaffected by confinement) and Z is the configurational partition function. The translational and rotational partition functions are available in the usual statistical mechanics texts $ ^{44,45} $ but are ultimately unimportant for the derivation that follows.

descriptor_candidates.name: conf_ratio_logASAvol
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: The entropy loss (in units of R) upon adsorption increases nonlinearly with the ratio of molecular accessible surface to molecular volume: compact, near-spherical molecules (low ASA/Vol) lose less entropy in confinement because they retain more rotational freedom, while elongated molecules (high ASA/Vol) lose more. Adding log(LabuteASA/Vol) as a nonlinear feature to the 14-input network will reduce the MAE of s_ads/s_gas prediction relative to the baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Confinement entropy loss is dominated by frustrated translational and rotational degrees of freedom (E01, E05). ASA/Vol is a shape factor inversely related to compactness: elongated molecules have more orientational constraints in a pore of fixed diameter, so configurational partition function volume shrinks more (E09). Log form reflects the logarithmic dependence of entropy on accessible configurational volume.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If a held-out evaluation shows the MAE of entropy loss/R does not decrease (or increases) when this descriptor is included alongside the 14 baseline inputs, or if the learned partial dependence of entropy loss on log(ASA/Vol) is not monotonically increasing over the majority of the data range, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: pore_mismatch confinement_descriptor
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss depends on the interplay between molecular rigidity/size (PBF) and the mismatch between pore-limiting and largest cavity diameters (lsd_p, lsd_f), scaled by accessible pore volume: frameworks where lsd_f is much larger than lsd_p (cage-like, window-separated pores) with small AV confine molecules most severely, so the descriptor correlates positively with entropy loss/R and improves MAE over the 14-input baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: In cage-window frameworks the molecule is locked in a cavity whose rotational/translational freedom is set by the window bottleneck (lsd_p) versus cavity size (lsd_f); E01 reports that TON (tubular, tight channels) gives the largest loss and FAU (large cages) the smallest, implying cavity-vs-window geometry controls entropy loss. PBF proxies molecular rigidity/planarity affecting how much vibrational/rotational entropy survives. Inference: no retrieved source states this combined descriptor; it is a new combination of known geometric effects.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If adding this descriptor does not lower MAE of entropy loss/R relative to the baseline, or if the sign of its learned effect on entropy loss is negative across the data, the hypothesis fails. Also falsified if AV alone already captures the same information (its inclusion with this descriptor yields no improvement).

descriptor_candidates.name: vol_density_entropic_descent
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Adsorption entropy loss scales with the degree of mass packing in the accessible pore (Vol*density on the source numerical scale, a proxy for framework compactness/occupiable volume per mass) modulated by molecular asphericity (PMI3/PMI1): framework compactness reduces entropy loss (open structures like FAU retain entropy, E01/E02) while aspheric molecules lose more; the product descriptor will reduce MAE of s_ads/s_gas prediction when added to the 14-input network.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: E02 reports that occupiable volume alone predicts entropy loss for zeolites; Vol*density on the source scale (no assigned physical units) similarly encodes framework openness/compactness. E01 shows entropy loss varies by framework, so a framework-openness term times a molecular anisotropy term (principal moment ratio, capturing rod-like vs. compact shapes that pack differently in pores) extends this known relation. The saturating log bounds the descriptor. Inference beyond the sources: the multiplicative coupling of asphericity with framework openness.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if including this descriptor fails to reduce MAE of entropy loss/R versus the 14-input baseline, or if learned sensitivity to PMI3/PMI1 is negligible (asphericity contribution absent), or if the effect of Vol*density does not dominate over noise across held-out frameworks.

descriptor_candidates.name: aspect_ratio_confinement
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R increases with the ratio of molecular longest-to-shortest principal moment (PMI3/PMI1, shape anisotropy) divided by accessible pore volume per gram (AV): elongated molecules in small-pore frameworks lose more rotational/translational entropy than compact molecules in large-pore frameworks, so this descriptor improves MAE of s_ads/s_gas over the 14-input baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: E01 shows entropy loss varies strongly with framework (TON largest, FAU smallest) and with molecular shape/confinement interplay; E07 reports molecular symmetry modulates confined motion. Rotational partition function suppression in confinement (E05: rotational degrees reduced by factor ~1.28; E09: configurational partition function governs entropy loss) should scale with asphericity when pore volume is small. Inference beyond sources: the specific multiplicative coupling of PMI3/PMI1 with 1/(AV+1) in log form.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If adding this descriptor to the 14-input network does not reduce MAE of entropy loss/R versus baseline (0.5638 R after round 2), or if the learned partial dependence on PMI3/PMI1 is non-monotonic/negligible, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: surface_packing_tightness
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R correlates with a packing-tightness descriptor combining molecular accessible surface per volume (LabuteASA/Vol) with framework-specific surface-to-density ratio (ASA/density): molecules with high surface-to-volume ratio adsorbed in frameworks with high surface area per unit density (tight, channel-dominated pores) experience larger configurational entropy loss, improving MAE over the baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: E01/E09 establish that configurational (translational+rotational) entropy loss dominates adsorption entropy and depends on confinement geometry; E02 shows a single material geometric descriptor (occupiable volume) largely predicts it. ASA (framework, m^2/g) and density together encode how finely divided the pore space is, while LabuteASA/Vol is the molecular shape factor from round 1 that showed near-baseline performance alone. Inference: their cross-product captures molecule-framework geometric matching not present in any single input.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if MAE of entropy loss/R does not decrease relative to the 14-input baseline, or if ablation shows the descriptor adds nothing beyond AV and LabuteASA already in the network (no marginal gain when either is shuffled).

descriptor_candidates.name: window_to_cavity_ratio_descriptor
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R rises with the squared ratio of largest cavity to pore-limiting diameter (lsd_f/lsd_p), a measure of cage-vs-window geometry, modulated by molecular elongation (GeDi/SPAN) and molecular mass (MW, via the Sackur-Tetrode mass dependence of gas-phase translational entropy): heavy, elongated molecules in cage-window frameworks lose the most entropy, and adding this descriptor reduces MAE of s_ads/s_gas below the baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: E01 derives gas-phase translational entropy with explicit mass dependence (Sackur-Tetrode), so MW enters the physical baseline of s_ads/s_gas; cage-window mismatch (lsd_f vs lsd_p) controls how much configurational volume survives (E09), and E04 shows pore-window geometry imposes shape-selective steric constraints. SPAN/GeDi capture molecular long-dimension vs. geometric deviation relevant to window passage (E10: molecules compress to pass windows ~80% of their size). Inference: the specific combination of cavity/window ratio with molecular size-shape terms is not in any retrieved source.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if including this descriptor fails to lower MAE of entropy loss/R versus the retained round-2 baseline, or if the learned effect of lsd_f/lsd_p has the wrong sign (larger ratio yielding smaller loss) across most of the data range.
